uncited: Inverse rendering and optimization recovers scene parameters (geometry, materials, lighting, or transfer functions) from observed images by minimizing a loss between rendered and target views.
Unlike forward rendering, which computes images from known parameters, this family solves an optimization problem where the rendering integral is differentiated with respect to scene variables.

It is distinguished from sibling methods like [Plenoxel Data Structure](930-plenoxel-data-structure.md) by its focus on parameter recovery rather than data representation, and from [Differentiable Depth Rendering](1332-differentiable-depth-rendering.md) by its primary output being semantic or physical scene properties rather than geometric depth maps.

The function signature is `double constant_intensity(double I0, double sigma, double q, double s)` where $I_0$ is initial intensity, $\sigma$ is absorption coefficient, $q$ is scattering parameter, and $s$ is path length.
Used to store results of a parameter search.
Used to store the final recovered parameters and error metrics.
Inverse rendering in volume visualization has evolved from manual transfer function design to automated, data-driven optimization.
The advent of differentiable rendering allowed gradients to flow from image loss to scene parameters, enabling end-to-end learning.
